newsitem.title: USA: L.A. municipal utility seeks charter amendments.
newsitem.headline: L.A. municipal utility seeks charter amendments.

text.p: The Los Angeles Department of Water & Power (LADWP) is counting on passage Tuesday of three local ballot initiatives to help the municipal utility make the transition to a competitive electricity industry.
Los Angeles voters are being asked to approve amendments to the utility's charter which would allow it to sell power outside the city limits and to expand investment and hiring options.
There is no organized opposition to the ballot proposals, according to LADWP and local media.

The municipal utility, the largest in the U.S. with 1.3 million customers, is burdened with a high debt load as well as high-cost generating assets, such as the Intermountain coal-fired power plant in Utah.
But LADWP has been moving to improve efficiency, including reducing its payroll by 20 percent over the past two years.

"We have always had the ability to market excess power," said LADWP spokesman Ed Freudenburg. "This (initiative) would allow us to get into competition the way the PUC (California Public Utilities Commission) is allowing investor-owned utilities to market energy."
Rather than market surplus power in the spot wholesale market, LADWP would like to sell power and other services under more lucrative, longer-term contracts, he explained.
Freudenburg noted that an exact timetable for the change, if approved by voters, would be decided by the Los Angeles city council.
Under the state's plan for investor-owned utilities, open competition would be phased in starting January 1998.

William McCarley, general manager of LADWP, who plans to leave his job by February, has said the municipal utility would seek a strategic alliance with a major energy company like Enron, Duke/Louis Dreyfus or PacifiCorp as part of its marketing strategy.
Earlier this month, Standard & Poor's lowered its rating on LADWP's $2.68 billion electric revenue bonds and refunding revenue bonds, reflecting the challenges of competition.
S&P noted the city council and the utility need to address the recovery of stranded costs and lower rates in order to become competitive.
In September, LADWP announced plans to give large industrial customers rate cuts totaling $25 million, but the proposal has languished at the city council.
Under the rate plan, about 70 percent of the municipal utility's industrial customers would see lower electricity bills, while about 20 percent would have rate increases of five percent or less.
